## Definition

The **range** is the simplest measure of dispersion, calculated as the difference between the maximum and minimum values in a dataset.

## Formula

$$\text{Range} = X_{max} - X_{min}$$

## Example

Dataset: 23, 45, 67, 89, 102

$$\text{Range} = 102 - 23 = 79$$

## Properties

| Property | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| Simple | Easy to calculate |
| Intuitive | Easy to understand |
| Sensitive to outliers | One extreme value affects it greatly |
| Ignores middle values | Only uses two data points |

## Advantages and Disadvantages

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
|------------|---------------|
| Quick to calculate | Highly sensitive to outliers |
| Easy to interpret | Ignores all middle values |
| Good for quick overview | Less informative than SD |

## When to Use

- Quick initial description of data
- Checking data entry (implausible range suggests errors)
- Reporting contest results (e.g., "scores ranged from 45 to 98")

## When Not to Use

- When outliers are present (use IQR instead)
- When precise measure of spread needed (use SD)
- For comparing variability across groups

## R Code Example

```r
# Calculate range
range(scores)  # Returns min and max

# Calculate difference
diff(range(scores))  # Returns range value

# Or manually
max(scores) - min(scores)
```

## Example with Outlier

```
Without outlier: 45, 48, 50, 52, 55
Range = 55 - 45 = 10

With outlier: 45, 48, 50, 52, 55, 150
Range = 150 - 45 = 105

One outlier dramatically changes the range!
```

## DataLab Connection

At **Reflex Test**, check the range of reaction times. Values outside a plausible range (e.g., < 100 ms or > 2000 ms) may indicate errors or inattention and might need to be excluded.
